rationale: The early-onset Parkinson review lists Mediterranean diet observational evidence and discusses rest tremor as a diagnostic sign. The cited Molsberry study reports diet patterns and prodromal features, and Mischley reports broad fresh-fruit intake and total PRO-PD severity. Neither cited result estimates raw fig intake against resting-tremor severity.

The review describes dietary sources of folate, folate metabolism, and homocysteine or vitamin interventions in neurodegenerative disease. Its clinical and mechanistic evidence provides no identifiable fig exposure or fig-linked rest-tremor measure.

This Personalized Parkinson Project analysis compares two-year daily-life sensor tremor measures with clinical rest tremor and patient-reported tremor, including analyses by medication status. It measures no fig intake and makes no food comparison.

The NHANES analysis relates physical activity to Parkinson prevalence and mortality. Energy, protein, carbohydrate and total fat intake enter a dietary adjustment model, with no raw-fig exposure or resting-tremor severity endpoint.

The original rat experiment compares canagliflozin with vehicle in a rotenone model and measures motor and gut outcomes. Sunflower oil is a vehicle. The study supplies no fig exposure or clinical resting-tremor result.

This review explicitly cites the 16-person Hegelmaier dietary pilot. Table 3 of that original (PMC7072275) lists figs in the common menu, without separate preparation, individual fig intake or rest-tremor scores. The review's separate 72-person SCFA and prebiotic study does not test fig intake.

The original body compares Parkinson and control brain tissue and uses cell models to study alpha-synuclein pathology and ferroptosis. Its experiments do not assign any food, and the measured outcomes do not include clinical resting-tremor change.

The experiments simulate electrical stimulation in a mathematical basal ganglia model. Clinical tremor motivates the simulation, without a participant-level dietary exposure or resting-tremor effect for fig.

The mouse comparison uses a high-fat diet and standard chow across transgenic and wild-type groups. The measured transcriptional adaptation and general Parkinson phenotype discussion supply no raw-fig intervention or human resting-tremor result.

This PPMI analysis classifies dysphagia through reported swallowing difficulty and the chewing-and-swallowing item. It compares patients with and without dysphagia on imaging and clinical domains that include rest tremor, without measuring fig intake or a food effect.

The study derives symbolic sequences from wrist acceleration during daily activities and assesses Parkinson motor state. The motor examination lists rest and postural tremor items separately. These clinical items are not linked to a fig dietary exposure.
Clinical follow-up compares rest-tremor item scores before and after unilateral pallidotomy, with arm and leg side specified. The exposure is surgery and there is no fig intake or dietary contrast.

Figure 4 measures scored resting tremor after oral whole-celery methanolic extract in MPTP mice. The botanical is Apium graveolens and has a separate related route for claim 0281. There is no Ficus exposure or human fig comparison.

The OCT study compares outer retinal thickness in Parkinson disease, dementia groups and matched controls. The exposure grouping and outcomes contain no raw-fig intake comparison or resting-tremor response.
The PPMI study uses Rasch analysis of repeated MDS-UPDRS II and III assessments to evaluate measurement precision. Tremor items are clinical scale observations without a fig exposure contrast.

The PPMI case-control analysis uses extrastriatal and striatal SPECT binding to examine serotonergic and dopaminergic involvement. It reports imaging and clinical correlations without assigning diet or estimating a fig-linked change in resting tremor.

The study follows asymmetry in motor signs and striatal dopamine transporter binding across 19 months of Parkinson disease. Its within-person imaging and motor comparisons offer no fig intake measure or diet-related rest tremor outcome.

This Parkinson and control observational study uses wearable accelerometry in clinic and daily life. Its sensor evaluation addresses mobility and motor symptom measurement without a fig dietary exposure or comparison.

The review follows the development of accelerometry, machine learning and other technologies for monitoring Parkinson motor symptoms. Tremor measurement examples address devices and algorithms, without a fig intervention or food-linked severity result.

Participants estimate body-part proportions in a visual task conducted by video call. The Parkinson/control comparison addresses body representation, without assigning figs or measuring a food-related tremor response.

This diagnostic study compares handwriting and striatal dopamine transporter imaging across Parkinson disease, essential tremor and control groups. It evaluates micrographia and has no raw-fig exposure or diet-related rest-tremor result.

The acoustic study compares vowel space and articulation in isolated REM sleep behavior disorder, early Parkinson disease and controls. Speech and imaging measures are separate from eating habits and no fig-related rest-tremor effect is reported.

This PPMI analysis clusters repeated clinical observations into Parkinson progression trajectories and considers symptomatic drug treatment. Motor trajectory differences have no fig intake measure or fig-related rest-tremor test.

The Personalized Parkinson Project analysis follows clinical focal and diffuse subtypes for two years. The reported motor progression and subtype changes are unlinked to a fig exposure or diet comparison.

The PPMI analysis relates multivariate MRI gray-matter measures to progression in total and subdomain MDS-UPDRS scores. The exposure is an imaging feature without a raw-fig comparison or diet-related resting-tremor result.
The mobile tests assess rest and postural tremor separately by accelerometry, using MDS-UPDRS references. The comparison evaluates measurement tools, without fig intake or a dietary outcome.

This PASADENA reanalysis compares the monoclonal antibody prasinezumab with placebo in early Parkinson disease and examines motor progression in candidate subgroups. The intervention is a drug and provides no raw-fig or diet-related rest-tremor estimate.

The deep-brain stimulation study relates stimulation anatomy to clinical change. Its tremor score sums postural, kinetic, resting amplitude and resting constancy items. No type of fig exposure is measured.
The systematic review evaluates vagus nerve stimulation for Parkinson disease and other movement disorders. Reported tremor findings are from stimulation protocols, without a fig dietary comparison.

The study models MRI changes and clinical progression, including a rest-tremor item correlation. The primary Personalized Parkinson Project analysis and PPMI replication use imaging and motor data without measuring fig intake.
Participants perform rapid isometric finger force pulses. The original examines segmentation during voluntary force generation, without a fig exposure or clinical dietary resting-tremor comparison.

This prospective pilot selects botulinum toxin injection sites using trunk angles and electromyography. Trunk misalignment and related symptoms are the treatment outcomes. It supplies no food comparison or change in rest tremor after fig.
The study compares wearable accelerometry with daily-life diaries on tremor, mobility, sleep and medication timing. The tremor diary has no fig intake variable or fig comparison.

This Personalized Parkinson Project study evaluates wrist photoplethysmographic signal quality and pulse rate, with rest tremor examined as a potential motion artifact. It contains no fig intake comparison or food effect on tremor.

The review discusses noradrenergic pathology and receptor imaging. It cites a thalamic receptor-binding association with tremor scores, without measuring raw-fig intake or a food-related symptom change.

This review studies Parkinson televisits, including agreement of remotely collected clinical information for tremor and other domains. The compared exposure is mode of assessment, with no fig-specific dietary result.

Accelerometry during a cognitive attention task and genetic risk scores were evaluated for distinguishing Parkinson disease from essential tremor. Measurement timing relates to medication intake and supplies no raw-fig or food comparison.

Parkinson, essential tremor and control participants perform a bimanual tapping task at two rates with and without auditory cues. The endpoint is tapping performance and task-associated kinetic tremor, with no fig exposure.

The study models candidate constituents of the multi-herb Yi-Gan-San formula, whose component list does not include Ficus. Network and molecular-docking predictions supply no human resting-tremor estimate after consuming fig.

The study compares a biomechanical system with observer ratings for Parkinson tremor at rest and with the arm outstretched. Test-retest reliability compares assessment methods and there is no fig dietary exposure.
